year 2000, nearly 17 million people living with disabilities have lost their vision every year, the most common cause being xerophthalmia.  In order to classify eye diseases effectively, a widely used approach involves collecting a large dataset of labeled images and training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).  However, this approach often struggles with a lack of sufficient labeled data and the exponential growth of parameters in deep neural networks.  To overcome these challenges, we introduce SwishNet, an innovative optimization framework that replaces the conventional activation function in CNNs with a smooth, element-wise function known as swish.  The swish activation function offers several advantages, including an adaptable shape that can be fine-tuned, which results in a reduced number of parameters in the network and improved convergence rates.  In addition, we develop the Lasso-Swish network by integrating the Lasso penalty with Swish activation, which significantly reduces overfitting in networks trained with limited labeled data.  Our proposed methods are experimentally validated on three ophthalmic datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of SwishNet in reducing parameters while outperforming conventional CNN networks.

neural networks develop spurious associations between their hidden layers and training data, thus compromising their reliability for model compression, pruning, and reverse engineering purposes. To address these concerns, we introduce the concept of self-regulation ability in neural networks and demonstrate that 2-Wasserbin loss, a variant of the 2-Wasserstein distance loss, endows a class of ReLU neural networks with self-regulation ability, effectively making them incapable of learning high-order spurious associations with the training data. weighted dominating set problem in bounded-diameter networks, where the weighted distance between nodes determines the cost of the decision variable. Our work targets weighted $\gamma$-dominating sets and achieves polynomial-sized solutions of size at most $O(\gamma n)$ for network diameters of at least $O(\log n)$. Notably, our algorithms provide constant-sized (i.e., $\gamma$-dominating) sets in networks with diameters of at least $O(\log h(n))$, where $h(n)$ denotes the smooth inverse of $n$. This is the first work to present a dominating set algorithm parameterized by the network diameter using the standard distributed computing model. Our primary algorithm achieves an $O(\gamma n)$-dominating set of size at most $O(\gamma n)$ within $O(\text{diam}(G))$ rounds. Additionally, we present secondary algorithms that improve upon this with an $O(\gamma n)$-dominating set of size at most $O(\gamma n \log^2 n)$ within $O(\text{diam}(G))$ rounds, and a set of size at most $O(\gamma n \log h(n))$ within $O(\text{diam}(G))$ rounds. All our algorithms achieve $O(\text{diam}(G))$ round complexities and use $O(\Delta)$ or $O(\log n)$ bit message sizes.

To minimize costs and enhance flexibility in inter-orbit communications, routers are replaced with store-and-forward nodes that limit data packet carriage. This study focuses on analyzing packet delivery within this type of limited-capability system, where each node only retains certain packet information and drops them after a certain number of hops. A random walk model is developed to represent packet movement and determine the conditions for packet loss, which can also apply to other protocols and topologies. Furthermore, the study examines how a packet's destination influences its probability of delivery and explores improving this through a model that considers this factor. Finally, simulations are conducted to verify the accuracy of the developed model.

We investigate the theoretical underpinnings of GRREM's success in learning fair representations and achieving relative risk minimization for risk measures encompassing Kelly utility, risk aversion, and Pareto optimality.  We prove that minimizing the max-composed convex combination of convex risk measures equivalent to solving a specific convex optimization problem with an $L_2$-regularization term.  The source of GRREM's favorable generalization properties is identified as the inherent $L_2$-regularization arising from the convex combination of risk measures. aims to locate and identify camouflaged objects within an image that contains camouflage patterns.  Due to the lack of publicly available datasets with annotated camouflage data, research in this area has been hindered.  Unsupervised semantic segmentation of the background in images becomes increasingly relevant, especially in the context of semantic segmentation datasets.  In this paper, we propose a two-stage framework consisting of a two-stream unsupervised semantic segmentation background segmentation stage and a COD stage.  During the first stage, we develop a novel content and style contrastive learning-based two-stage unsupervised semantic segmentation framework to accurately segment the background.  During the second stage, we design a reference-guided dual-attention decoder module which fuses the pre-trained encoder features with the segmented mask features, leveraging the reference information effectively.  Moreover, our framework can be simplified by removing the middle stage, yielding a direct outcome equivalent to the COD task.  Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed COD stage significantly outperforms the unsupervised semantic segmentation framework and state-of-the-art COD methods.  Furthermore, our proposed method achieves superior performance when applied to publicly available datasets.

  binary classification tasks, extending them to multi-class classification
  remains a challenging issue.  The issue is compounded by the absence of
  negative samples, which are necessary to capture complex relationships
  between positive and negative samples.  The absence of such samples
  significantly hampers the ability of neural networks to model a class as
  a unified whole.  The work presented here explores a novel approach,
  entitled external negative generation, to address this limitation.  The
  approach proposes to leverage known class characteristics and boundary
  information from external sources to automatically produce negative
  samples for each class, thereby eliminating the need for manual
  intervention.  The external negative generation is then incorporated
  into a modified support vector machine framework, adapting it to handle
  multi-class classification tasks, with the goal of balancing simplicity,
  interpretability, and performance.  The effectiveness of the proposed
  approach has been validated on three face recognition datasets, ZOSR,
  FERET and MS1M, where it outperformed existing methods, achieving the best
  results for several benchmark protocols.  The source code for the project
  is available on GitHub at

Our analysis shows that solutions to the transport equation along such flow lines are necessarily constant, provided the flow's regularity is within $F^{s,1}_{p,1}$ where the index $s$ is greater than $d+2\delta_P$ with $2\delta_P$ being the Hardy-relativistic exponent related to $p$.  Moreover, we demonstrate that these results are optimal regarding the admissible smoothness of the distribution.  Distributions with this level of singularity can give rise to causal commuting flows that have non-constant solutions.  This connection is further illustrated by the construction of flow lines as integral manifolds of a single vector field, where that field commutes causally but is not itself causal.  Such a construction is possible provided the distribution is an extension of Folland-Stein spaces by $H^{s-\12\delta_P}_{p,p}$ with comparable lower bounds for the required index.

Wittenberg identified a class of orders within rank one cubic fields, characterized by a specific property where prime ideals with norm $p$ and inert behavior in a quadratic subfield $p^{2}p'\pi'$ have order one. Since 2004, research has expanded on this, with multiple studies building on and applying this criterion. This survey aims to gather all known related findings, beginning with an explanation of the underlying concepts, before comprehensively listing all orders with the rank one property for rank one cubic fields, with references to previous work available on computer.

This is achieved by employing a path integral approach to derive an effective Hamiltonian for any given polymer configuration, regardless of its self-intersection density.  The dynamics of this effective Hamiltonian are governed by a non-linear stochastic differential equation, the responses of which to various potentials reflect those of all underlying polymers, independent of their specific movement history.  A change in solvent strength corresponds to an alteration in noise intensity, and we find that polymers exhibiting coil behavior follow an effective dimension that is neither integer nor fractional.  This effective Hamiltonian framework provides the basis for analyzing complex polymer behaviors, and we use it to investigate a previously unexplored regime of high-density, strongly interacting polymers.  By estimating an effective hydrodynamic radius and gyration size through the calculation of their distribution functions, we obtain general insights into polymer self-interaction and find that this effective radius grows linearly with the hydrodynamic radius in its undilated state.

  neutrino research, nonetheless the vast potential of this field remains
  largely unrealized.  As the community shrinks, small-scale neutrino
  experiments offer an ideal opportunity to drive future developments.  To
  ensure their success, it is crucial to accurately assess the performance
  of these systems and in particular to understand how to model the complex

  current single-neutrino simulations fall short of their potential due to

  which can be applied to almost any type of neutrino detector.  Using this

  fully integrate these simulations into the analysis chain for small-scale

  thickened walls, is a key radiological finding in emphysema. Airway
  wall indices are calculated to quantify this radiological observation.
  However, their reliable computation requires matching CT images with MR
  images of the same patient, which proves challenging due to the disparity
  in imaging modalities and image quality issues in low-resolution MR images.
  This research tackles these challenges by focusing on accurate airway
  segmentation and subsequent quantification tasks.  A novel framework is
  proposed to perform airway segmentation in combined CT-MR images and is
  further extended for quantitative analysis.  The framework leverages
  mutual information to enhance airway segmentation performance and utilizes
  a two-stage approach to mitigate membrane noise influencing AWAs calculations.
  The framework's effectiveness was validated using a custom synthetic
  dataset and real low-resolution MR images, compared to a baseline purely
  RC-based model.  The proposed framework significantly improved airway
  segmentation precision, resulting in more accurate computations of AWAs.
